children: WASHINGTON-Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito will sit out a major case on climate change, a surprising about-face for the conservative justice after he resisted calls earlier this year to recuse himself over his energy-stock ownership.

Alito's decision means that only eight justices will hear a dispute about whether local governments can sue fossil-fuel companies over damages allegedly caused by climate change. The closely watched case will be argued on Oct. 5, the first day of the high court's new term.
Alito didn't explain his recusal, which was revealed Monday in a one-sentence letter from the court's clerk to the lawyers on both sides of the case. Alito didn't respond to a request for comment.

Alito owns shares of several oil-and-gas companies, and he has recused himself from prior cases involving those companies. But according to his financial-disclosure forms, Alito doesn't own shares in the two companies that are defendants in the climate-change case: Suncor Energy and ExxonMobil. Local officials in Boulder, Colo., are trying to bring a lawsuit against those companies to trial. The companies say the Constitution and federal law bars the lawsuit and dozens of other similar cases brought by local governments around the country.

Alito had been considered a probable vote to shut down the climate lawsuits. Without him, the companies likely need all five of the court's remaining conservative justices, because a 4-4 tie would leave in place a lower-court ruling that allowed Boulder's lawsuit to move forward. Legal experts are eyeing two conservatives in particular-Justices Clarence Thomas and Neil Gorsuch-who are often hostile to environmental claims but have in the past expressed skepticism that federal law can implicitly override state law, which is what the oil companies are arguing.

In May, after the court agreed to take up the Colorado case, some environmental advocates and left-leaning groups called for Alito to step aside. They argued the court's eventual ruling would affect similar lawsuits against companies in which Alito does own stock, such as ConocoPhillips and Phillips 66.
The Supreme Court's legal counsel advised Alito at the time that he wasn't ethically required to recuse because he didn't have a financial interest in the case.
Gabe Roth, the executive director of Fix the Court, which advocates for stricter judicial ethics rules, said Monday that Alito should explain why he decided to recuse himself after all.
